title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1)
hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk

segments.voice: Yesterday, go'el, the redeemer. Your line was the outsider in the line.

"How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee." That's a priest, speaking to a woman at prayer. His name is Eli, and he's sitting by a post of the temple of the LORD at Shiloh, watching her. Her lips are moving. No sound comes out. So he decides she's had too much at the family's meal. He couldn't be more wrong. The first book of Samuel doesn't open with a king or a battle. It opens with a woman who can't have children, a family trip to worship, and a prayer so deep it looks like a scandal.

Back up. Hannah's husband, Elkanah, has two wives. "Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children." Every year at Shiloh, the text says, her rival provoked her sore, until Hannah wept and couldn't eat. Elkanah loves her, and tries: "Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" Yesterday the women told Naomi that Ruth was better than seven sons. Here a husband asks if he's better than ten, and the text gives no answer from her. Hannah gets up and goes to pray. "She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." She vows: if God will remember her and give her a son, she'll give him back to the LORD all his life. Then: "Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken." When he scolds her, she doesn't flinch. "No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." Poured out, like water from a jar, nothing kept back. Eli changes his mind at once: "Go in peace," and may God grant your petition. And here's the detail to carry: Hannah goes and eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." She isn't pregnant yet. Nothing has changed. Only the jar is empty. Later she has a son and names him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD." And she keeps her vow.
screen: `AM NOT I BETTER TO THEE THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: Let whatever's heaviest come up, the thing you want and don't have, the thing that keeps hurting, without shaping it into sentences; Hannah's voice wasn't heard. Let your breath carry it out slowly, like tipping a jar until it's empty, and notice what's left. If you pray, do this before God.
Hannah's prayer. A silent prayer at Shiloh, so deep the priest thought she was drunk. She poured out her soul before the LORD, and went home no more sad.
Your line: poured out before the lord. Her face changed before anything else did. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Hannah's story when they pray about longing, infertility or grief, and read her silent prayer in 1 Samuel 1 alongside her song of thanks in 1 Samuel 2.

fork.setup: you're Hannah, praying silently at Shiloh. the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you say?
options: no, my lord. I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
tell him off for judging a stranger.
fork.reveal: she answers him plainly: a woman of a sorrowful spirit, not drunk, pouring out her soul. and Eli blesses her.

chat.says: When Eli thought Hannah was drunk, what was she actually doing?
options: Praying silently, pouring out her soul before the LORD; only her lips moved.
Singing quietly, since the priests didn't allow women to pray aloud.
Weeping over a fight with Elkanah, who had told her to stop praying.
chat.meaning: Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved. She told Eli: I have poured out my soul before the LORD.

Shiloh.meaning: where the family went every year to worship

Samuel.meaning: Hannah's son: because I have asked him of the LORD

notes: Audit: all KJV quotations checked against the 1769 text; no changes needed.
Eli 'sitting on a seat by a post of the temple of the LORD' follows 1 Samuel 1:9. 'Every year' follows 1:7 ('as he did so year by year').
The vow (1:11) is paraphrased, not quoted.
'Like water from a jar' is an image for 'poured out', not a claim about the Hebrew word.
Trapdoor floor 3: Samuel anoints Saul (1 Samuel 10:1) and David (16:13); 'Israel's first kings' summarizes those. Confirm.
The contrast between Ruth 4:15 ('better than seven sons') and 1 Samuel 1:8 ('better than ten sons') is the narrator's own linking of two texts.
